teach.title: What it does
teach.say: Put a gerundive beside a part of *sum* and Latin has said 'must'. That is **the gerundive with sum (the 'must be done' pattern: liber legendus est = the book must be read)**. *Hic liber hodiē legendus est* — this book must be read today. There is no separate word for 'must'; the *-nd-* and the *est* carry it between them.

check.ask: What does edendus est say about the food?

teach.title: It agrees with the thing that must be done
teach.say: The gerundive is an adjective, so it takes the gender, number and case of the subject, and *sum* takes the number too: *liber legendus est*, *epistulae scrībendae sunt*, *vāsa lavanda sunt*, *puerī laudandī sunt*. Find the subject first and the ending follows from it.

check.ask: vāsa is neuter plural. Fill in the gerundive of lavō to match it.

teach.title: With no subject at all: 'one must'
teach.say: When nothing in particular has to be done — only an action — Latin uses the neuter singular with *est* and no subject at all: *dormiendum est* 'one must sleep', *tacendum est* 'one must keep quiet'. English needs a word like 'one' or 'we'; Latin needs none.

check.ask: tacendum est has no subject at all. What is this construction?

teach.title: Not the perfect passive
teach.say: *scrīpta est* and *scrībenda est* look alike and mean opposite things. The perfect passive *scrīpta est* says the letter has been written and the job is done; the gerundive *scrībenda est* says it still must be written. Look for the *-nd-*.

check.ask: pūniendus est: has the slave been punished, or must he be?

teach.title: Only sum changes tense
teach.say: The gerundive itself never changes its tense; the verb beside it does. *Porta claudenda est* — the door must be shut. *Porta claudenda erat* — it had to be shut. *Crās vīlla aedificanda erit* — tomorrow the house will have to be built. Change the part of *sum* and you have moved the obligation in time.

check.ask: erit puts the obligation in the future. Fill in the gerundive of aedificō to match vīlla.

teach.title: Say it yourself
teach.say: Name the thing that must be done, match the gerundive to it, and add the right part of *sum*: *haec verba*, neuter plural, gives *haec verba omnia discenda sunt* — all these words must be learnt.

check.ask: verba is neuter plural. Fill in the gerundive of discō.

core.text: Put the gerundive (the '-nd-' adjective: 'to be done'; aqua bibenda = water to be drunk) next to a form of *sum* (to be) and you get **the gerundive with sum (the 'must be done' pattern: liber legendus est = the book must be read)**. *Cibus comedendus est* — the food must be eaten; *tacendum est* — one must be silent (no subject, so the neuter *-um*). Latin name: *coniugātiō periphrastica passīva*.
English: *the food is to be eaten*, *it must be eaten*. Think 'has to be done', then say it naturally: *we have to eat the food*.
Gerundive agreeing with the subject + sum = must / ought to be; neuter -ndum est with no subject = one must; in reported speech -ndum esse.

invented.en: The letter must be written today.

core.text: *laudātus est* — the perfect passive (the 'was done / has been done' form: laudatus est), he was praised — and *laudandus est* (he must be praised) share the shape participle + *est*. Look at the participle: *-tus / -sus* is the perfect passive participle (done); *-ndus* is the gerundive, to be done. *victus est* = was beaten; *vincendus est* = must be beaten.

more.text: The tense of *sum* moves the duty in time: *pūniendus erat* — had to be punished. The person who must do it is added in the dative (the 'to/for' form), not with ā/ab: *liber mihi legendus est* — I must read the book. See the dative of agent lesson.

The learner's notes: the future passive participle is commonly joined with a form of *sum* to make a short sentence about what needs to be done (*aqua bibenda est*, the water needs drinking), and just as often sits inside an accusative + infinitive clause with *esse*: *sciō cibum comedendum esse* — I know the food needs eating; *intellegis vōcem audiendam esse*.

Ørberg's chapter 31: *discipulus industrius magistrō laudandus est; discipulus piger reprehendendus et pūniendus est; tacendum est; Lingua Latīna vōbīs discenda est; quidquid magister imperāvit discipulō faciendum est; dominus dīcit ovēs bene cūrandās esse.* With a verb that takes no object the pattern is always the impersonal neuter: *eundum est* (one must go), *pugnandum est*, *dēspērandum nōn est*. The Latin name means 'the roundabout passive conjugation'; Cato's *Carthāgō dēlenda est* (Carthage must be destroyed) is the famous case.
